title: Kisor v. Wilkie (2019)
summary: Kisor retained Auer deference to an agency’s interpretation of its own genuinely ambiguous regulation, while requiring rigorous interpretation, a reasonable agency reading, and authoritative, expert, fair, considered judgment. The judgment below was vacated and remanded.
notes: The judgment was unanimous (vacated and remanded) but the doctrine survived only 5-4: Justice Kagan wrote; Chief Justice Roberts concurred in part; Justice Gorsuch concurred in the judgment only (joined by Thomas, and by Kavanaugh and Alito in part), arguing Auer should be overruled; Justice Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment joined by Alito. The Court faulted the Federal Circuit for declaring the regulation ambiguous without first exhausting the traditional tools of construction.

sections.Parties: James Kisor, a Vietnam veteran, sought retroactive disability benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs. The Secretary represented the agency. The dispute concerned the VA’s interpretation of its own rule for reconsidering claims when previously unconsidered service records become available. (Printed 987–988.)
sections.Material Facts:
Kisor applied in 1982 for benefits based on post-traumatic stress disorder arising from Operation Harvest Moon. The VA’s psychiatrist recorded his participation in the operation but concluded that he did not have PTSD, and the agency denied benefits. Kisor reopened the claim in 2006 with a new psychiatric report. The VA then accepted the diagnosis but awarded benefits from the reopening date. (Printed 987.)

The regulation permitted retroactive benefits based on relevant official service-department records not considered in the original denial. Kisor produced two records confirming participation in the operation. A single Board of Veterans’ Appeals adjudicator deemed them irrelevant because the original denial rested on the absence of PTSD, rather than uncertainty about the military event. Kisor argued that relevance could extend to any criterion for benefits, including an uncontested one. The meaning of “relevant” therefore determined whether these records could support retroactivity. (Printed 987–988.)
sections.Procedural History:
The Board upheld the agency’s timing determination, and the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims affirmed its reasoning. The Federal Circuit also affirmed, holding the regulation ambiguous and deferring under Auer because it regarded both readings as reasonable. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on whether to overrule Auer and Seminole Rock. (Printed 988.)

The lower court had insufficiently exhausted interpretive tools and too readily assumed that the Board member’s interpretation warranted deference. The Supreme Court did not determine Kisor’s ultimate entitlement to retroactive benefits.
sections.Issue: Should the Court overrule deference to an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations? If the doctrine remains, what must a reviewing court establish before giving an agency’s reading controlling weight, and had the Federal Circuit adequately performed that inquiry? (Printed 987–993; supplementary Part IV.)
sections.Holding: Auer and Seminole Rock were retained, with their limits clarified and strengthened. Five Justices joined Parts I, II-B, III-B, and IV: the background, operational limits on deference, stare decisis rationale, and remand. Only four joined Parts II-A and III-A, which supply the broader affirmative defense of the doctrine and responses to statutory and constitutional challenges. The controlling limits require genuine ambiguity after exhausting interpretive tools, a reasonable reading within that ambiguity, and an agency interpretation that is authoritative, grounded in relevant expertise, and fair and considered. (Printed 987, 990–995, 1000.)
sections.Reasoning:
Part II-B requires the court to interpret first. Difficulty on a first reading and the parties’ disagreement do not establish genuine ambiguity. The court must examine the regulation using the usual legal tools. If a single reasonable meaning emerges, the court enforces it. If ambiguity persists, the agency’s reading must stay within the range the court identifies. Deference cannot permit the agency to create a new regulation under the guise of interpretation. (Printed 990–991.)

The court then examines who issued the interpretation, in what form, and in what substantive setting. The interpretation must represent an authoritative agency position, though it need not personally come from the agency head. It must draw on relevant agency expertise and reflect considered judgment. A convenient litigation position, a post hoc justification, or a change imposing unfair surprise on regulated parties fails that inquiry. The opinion treats interpretations first offered in briefs cautiously, while explaining the particular circumstances in which Auer itself accepted a requested amicus view from an agency that was not a party. (Printed 991–992.)

Part III-B preserves the doctrine through stare decisis, emphasizing the long chain of decisions and settled regulatory constructions. Chief Justice Roberts supplied the decisive fifth vote for that part and for the doctrinal limits. He considered the practical distance from persuasive-weight review relatively small, while expressly distinguishing a duty to defer under specified conditions from persuasion alone. He also distinguished interpretation of regulations from the separate Chevron question about statutes. (Printed 994–996.)

Justice Kagan’s four-Justice portions defend agency primacy through the agency’s knowledge of its own regulations, subject expertise, political accountability, and the value of uniformity. They read § 706 as compatible with reasonableness review and maintained that deference does not make an interpretive rule independently enforceable: the underlying legislative rule supplies the legal obligation. These explanations should not be described as five-Justice holdings. (Printed 989–990, 992–994.)

Justice Gorsuch concurred in the judgment while arguing that §§ 706 and 553 require independent legal interpretation and prevent agencies from obtaining binding effect for new interpretations without required rulemaking procedures. Justice Thomas joined his opinion, Justice Kavanaugh joined Parts I–V, and Justice Alito joined Parts I–III. Justice Kavanaugh, joined by Justice Alito, separately favored overruling Auer and argued that rigorous use of interpretive tools would usually identify the best meaning; genuine open-ended policy choices would instead be reviewed under State Farm. The assigned notes preserve the tension with later Loper Bright reasoning without treating Kisor as overruled. (Printed 996–1002.)

topics.lrs-i-regulatory-deference: Kisor supplies the controlling prerequisites for deference to an agency’s own regulation.
topics.lrs-i-persuasive-weight: Roberts distinguishes Kisor’s conditional controlling weight from Skidmore persuasion even where they overlap in practice.
topics.lrs-i-statutes-and-regulations: The source distinguishes the regulatory-interpretation holding from later Loper Bright statutory review.
topics.lrs-i-delegated-discretion: Kavanaugh separates legal meaning from reasonable policy choices within an open-ended regulatory grant.
topics.lrs-i-statutory-stare-decisis: Kisor's retention of Auer rested expressly on stare decisis, the counterpoint to Loper Bright's willingness to overrule Chevron.
